summary: SPHEREx Blink is a free web app that lets anyone pick a spot in the sky and flip through every image NASA's SPHEREx telescope has taken of it, oldest to newest, so objects that move or change brightness stand out. It is a modern version of the blink comparator Clyde Tombaugh used to find Pluto in 1930. The user explores an all-sky SPHEREx map, clicks a target or types RA and Dec, and the site pulls every matching exposure live from NASA's IRSA archive, removes the zodiacal light, and lines the frames up north-up so they play like a video. Four views (every image, visit stacks, differences and detector stacks) cover all six detectors and 102 bands from 0.75 to 5 µm. A spectrum is built from every image, and Gaia DR3 and AllWISE overlays and SPHEREx quality flags help tell real movers from known stars and bad pixels. On Barnard's Star the site loads 358 exposures from six visits, and the difference view shows the star's 10.4″ per year motion as an amber and blue pair. New SPHEREx data releases are picked up automatically, every view has a shareable link and embed code, and help icons and a guided tour make it usable by students as well as astronomers.
details:
1. What SPHEREx Blink does

SPHEREx Blink is a website for watching the infrared sky change. It opens on an all-sky map made from SPHEREx data. The user drags and zooms around the sky, picks one of 16 marked targets (including all five challenge test targets), clicks any other spot, or types RA and Dec in decimal degrees or sexagesimal. The site then opens a full-screen blink viewer that loads every SPHEREx exposure of that position and plays them in date order.

Stars that stay put look steady. A nearby star, a brown dwarf or an asteroid shifts from frame to frame, and a variable star flickers. This is the blink comparator technique that Clyde Tombaugh used to discover Pluto in 1930, rebuilt for the SPHEREx archive and for any web browser.


2. The problem it solves

SPHEREx maps the whole sky every six months in 102 infrared bands from 0.75 to 5 µm. Objects that move or vary only show up when images of the same spot are compared over time. But the data is stored as separate exposures, each a 2040 × 2040 pixel file of about 4 MB, taken at its own roll angle. One 0.1° field around Barnard's Star already has 358 exposures. Comparing them by hand means querying the archive, cutting out the field and reprojecting every image, which is a programming job. SPHEREx Blink does all of that in a few seconds, with no code and no software to install.

Sky map: All-sky SPHEREx map in colour, made from three wavelengths (1.25, 2.19 and 3.29 µm).

Coordinate input: RA and Dec in decimal degrees or sexagesimal. Five test targets plus 11 more are one click away.

Every image: Each exposure in date order, 0.5 to 20 frames a second, with keyboard stepping.

Visit stacks: Exposures more than 20 days apart start a new visit. Each visit is averaged to cut noise.

Differences: Each visit minus the mean of all the others. Amber is brighter in this visit, blue was brighter in the others. A mover shows as an amber and blue pair, a variable as one colour.

Detector stacks: Everything each of the six detectors saw, averaged. The deepest view in each wavelength range.

Detector filter: All detectors or one of D1 to D6, each shown with its wavelength range and image count.

Spectrum: Flux in mJy against wavelength, built on the fly from every loaded image. Click a point to open its image, or download as CSV.

Overlays: Gaia DR3 stars moved to each image's date using proper motion, AllWISE sources, SPHEREx quality flags, target crosshair and spectrum aperture.

Image facts: Date, detector, exact wavelength, data release, observation ID, exposure time, quality check, PSF width, glow contamination, and cosmic-ray, snowball and satellite-streak counts.

Field of view: 0.05°, 0.1°, 0.2° or 0.3°.

Share and embed: Every view has its own link carrying the coordinates, field of view, view and detector, plus iframe code for other websites.

Help: 23 help icons explain every control and technical field. A 14-step guided tour walks new users through the site.

New data: The site asks IRSA once a day which SPHEREx collections exist and searches all of them, so new data releases appear with no code change.


3. How it works

  1. Search. The server uses astroquery to ask IRSA's image search service (SIA2) for every SPHEREx exposure within 1″ of the position, across every data release it has discovered.
  2. Cut out. IRSA's server-side cutout service returns 1.5 times the field of view, so the field stays covered at any roll angle. Each cutout is about 125 kB. The 4 MB original is never downloaded.
  3. Clean and align. The zodiacal light model that ships with each image (the ZODI layer) is subtracted from the IMAGE layer. astropy and reproject then put every frame onto one north-up, east-left grid centred on the target. The quality FLAGS layer goes onto the same grid, and the exact wavelength at the target is read from the image's wavelength lookup table.
  4. Stream. The server fetches 12 cutouts at once and sends each frame down one connection the moment it is ready, as 16-bit pixels plus one flag byte per pixel, about 10 kB per frame. Frames are requested round-robin across visits and detectors, so the first few already span every visit and blinking is useful within seconds.
  5. In the browser. Visit stacks, differences and detector stacks are averages of the loaded frames. The spectrum sums the flux within 2 pixels of the aperture and subtracts the median of a 4 to 7 pixel ring around it.

The backend is Python (FastAPI, astropy, astroquery, reproject). The frontend is plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no build step, and uses Aladin Lite for the sky map.

4. Results on real SPHEREx data

We tested the site on Barnard's Star, the star with the largest proper motion in the sky (10.4″ a year).

The 358 exposures fall into six visits between 15 August 2025 and 22 September 2026. In the Differences view, visit 3 (113 images from 11 March to 10 April 2026) minus the mean of the other 245 images leaves an amber and blue pair exactly at the star's position, while the fixed background stars cancel out. That pair is the star's motion, seen directly in SPHEREx data.

IRSA answers about a third of cutout requests with "503 Server busy", so each request is retried up to 7 times. Everything is cached, so a second visit to a field is instant. The code is covered by 34 automated tests, all passing.

5. Design

The interface is black and white, with hairlines, square corners and monospaced readouts, like a laboratory instrument. Colour is used only for data: the sky itself, the six detectors, the amber and blue of the difference images, and one amber marker for the selected spot. Nothing in the interface competes with the images.

6. Benefits and goals

  • Students and the public can open a famous star and watch it move in real NASA data, with no code.
  • Astronomers can check any field for motion or variability in seconds instead of writing a script.
  • Teachers and outreach sites can share a link or embed a live view in a web page.
  • The mission gets a viewer that keeps up with it, because new data releases appear automatically.

Next steps: search by object name, automatic flagging of likely movers from the difference images, cross-checks against more catalogues, and a way for users to mark and share candidates so the public can help search the sky.

We used Claude (Anthropic), through Claude Code, as an assistant to help write and test the website's backend code, interpret data, and to help draft the slide deck. The team directed the work, reviewed it and tested the site. No AI-generated images, video or audio are used. Every image and number shown comes from real SPHEREx data served by NASA/IPAC IRSA.
